newsitem.title: INDIA: India's central bank seen easing money soon.
newsitem.headline: India's central bank seen easing money soon.

text.p: India's central bank is expected to announce steps to ease money conditions and boost exports in the hope of reviving a sagging econony, analysts said on Thursday.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) policy for second half 1996/97 (April-March) would be released on Saturday, officials said.
"As data on real economic activity come in weaker than expected, monetary policy is likely to be easier," said Bidisha Ganguly, economist at Kotak Securities.
Analysts say the economic slowdown is due to last year's high interest rates which compelled industry to postpone investment decisions.
"Corporates postponed investment decisions last year in a big way as interest rates were too high," said the treasury head of a private bank. "Consequently, demand for bank funds is lower this year."
Latest Industry Ministry figures showed that India's 24-sector industrial production index rose just 5.6 percent during April-August 1996 against 12.6 percent a year ago.

A cut in banks' cash reserve requirements would ease money conditions and spark a fall in interest rates, analysts said. Prime lending rates range between 15.5 percent for leading state-run banks and 19 percent for foreign and private banks. Last year prime lending rates were between 16.5 and 20 percent.

"Given an inflation rate of 6.34 percent (as measured by the wholesale price index in September), the rates being charged by banks are high," said Aashish Pitale, manager debt research at ICICI Securities and Finance Company.
"We have to remember that the prime lending rates that most banks offer do not reflect the actual cost of funds for most borrowers," he said.
Typically, the actual rates charged to most borrowers would be a mark-up of 100-200 basis points over prime lending rate, he said.
The exports sector, which is performing poorly this year, would also require the RBI's attention, analysts said.

The Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy, an independent Bombay-based think tank, said in its September review of the economy that exports grew by 10 percent in April-August 1996 against 28 percent in the same 1995 period.
Bankers said they expected a cut in the refinance rates charged by the RBI against export credit.
Banks lend to exporters at 13 percent per annum and are allowed to draw refinance against their export credit disbursements from the RBI at a rate of 11 percent per annum.
"A cut in the refinance rate to 10 percent will help us reduce our export finance rate to 12 percent," said a banker.
